# Component catalogue

This catalogue lists every third-party component the product is built from or runs on: the packages, libraries, container images, Helm charts, tools and GitHub Actions. For each one it says what the component provides, why the architecture needs it, the exact version or digest that is pinned, where it is used, and how it fits the compliance requirements.

Nothing here is typed by hand. The pages are generated from the compliance fit register, [`compliance/resources.json`](https://github.com/VitalPointAI/near-ai-vscode/blob/main/compliance/resources.json), which CI checks against what the repository really uses. A component cannot be added without a reviewed entry, and an entry cannot stay after the component is removed. The same register produces the component inventory in the assessor package.

This catalogue is evidence for these controls in the compliance package: CM-8 and CM-8(1) (the inventory, kept current with each change), CM-7 (why each component is needed), SA-4 (the review before a component is used), SA-5 (this documentation) and SR-3 (exact pins). It is evidence only: your organization decides what it accepts.

There are 160 components in 10 areas. The role of 23 of them is waiting for the owner to confirm it; each says so.

## How to read an entry

- **Scope** says whether the component runs in the product (runtime), or is only used to build or test it.
- **Compliance fit** is the register's verdict. "Pass with conditions" means the component may be used only as its conditions say; they are listed under the entry.
- **Air gap** says whether it works with no internet access. Software for a hosted site always arrives as a signed offline bundle.
- **Controls** are the controls the component helps with or affects.

## Areas

### [Workbench, sessions and extension](./workbench.md)

This is what people use. The extension is the agent team inside the editor: chat, Team Studio, the Staff Room and its map. It ships no node\_modules, so the few libraries it needs are copied into the package at fixed versions and reviewed (the vendored entries in this area). The workbench is a browser-based editor built on Eclipse Theia that runs the same extension. At a hosted site, Theia Cloud starts one workbench session for each person after they sign in.

### [Sync hub and relay](./sync-and-relay.md)

The sync hub lets several people share staff and project work. Your organization runs it itself, as a container. The relay is a separate small service for chats that arrive from outside the editor; today it is only a foundation and carries no messages yet. Both are built into minimal images with no shell or package manager.

3 components: npm:jose, image:docker.io/bbernhard/signal-cli-rest-api, image:gcr.io/distroless/nodejs26-debian13.

### [Site platform: Kubernetes, registry, ingress and certificates](./site-platform.md)

Every hosted site runs the same platform. RKE2 is the Kubernetes the rest runs on. Software arrives as a signed offline bundle and is loaded into the site's own registry (Zot, or Harbor at larger sites), so nothing is pulled from the internet. Kyverno refuses any image that is not signed with your organization's key. HAProxy is the one entry point for people, and cert-manager issues every certificate from the site's own certificate authority.

### [Identity and sign-in](./identity.md)

Keycloak signs people in with passkeys or hardware security keys only; there are no passwords. Its settings are applied from the repository as code, and its data sits in a PostgreSQL database we build ourselves. oauth2-proxy sits in front of each workbench session, so a session is reached only after sign-in.

6 components: image:docker.io/adorsys/keycloak-config-cli, image:quay.io/keycloak/keycloak, image:registry.access.redhat.com/ubi9/go-toolset, image:registry.access.redhat.com/ubi9/ubi-minimal, chart:keycloakx, tool:postgresql.

### [Secrets and keys](./secrets-and-keys.md)

OpenBao holds each site's secrets and keys, and the site's internal certificate authority that cert-manager issues from. Where the site has a hardware security module (HSM), OpenBao is sealed with a key held in it, through the kms-pkcs11 plugin. SoftHSM2 is a software stand-in used only in the lab and in tests.

5 components: image:quay.io/openbao/openbao-ubi, image:registry.access.redhat.com/ubi9/ubi, chart:openbao, tool:kms-pkcs11, tool:softhsm2.

### [Storage, logging and monitoring](./storage-logging-monitoring.md)

Longhorn gives the site encrypted storage for workspaces, databases and logs. Fluent Bit collects logs and audit records from every node and sends them to OpenSearch at the site; nothing is sent outside. Prometheus collects metrics about the nodes and Kubernetes, which the load tests read.

### [Release and supply chain](./release-and-supply-chain.md)

These pieces turn a reviewed commit into a release you can trust. GitHub Actions build and test every change. The release workflow packages the extension, records checksums and signed provenance, and writes a software bill of materials (SBOM) for each image. cosign signs what we build with your organization's key, and hauler packs the signed images and charts into the offline bundle a site imports.

## Software bill of materials

This catalogue covers the direct components that someone chose and reviewed. A software bill of materials (SBOM) is the machine-readable list of everything inside a shipped file, including every package those components pull in. Use the catalogue to understand why each part is there; use the SBOM to check exactly what a release contains.

Each release keeps its SBOMs with the release itself, in CycloneDX JSON:

- **The extension package (VSIX)** carries `extension/sbom.cdx.json`: every third-party package the extension ships, and the bundled map data. The release workflow builds it with the package.
- **The assessor package** (`compliance-package-<version>.tar.gz` on the GitHub release) carries the same file as `evidence/bundle/vsix-sbom.cdx.json`, and the relay image SBOM that Syft writes as `evidence/relay-image-sbom.json`.
- **The images we rebuild for a hosted site** each get a Syft SBOM. When an image is published from a release tag, its SBOM is attached to it as a signed GitHub attestation.
- **The workbench image** has no SBOM of its own yet. It is planned with the Phase 46 work that also signs that image.

To get the SBOMs of one release, for example version 0.4.38, with the [GitHub CLI](https://cli.github.com/):

```sh
gh release download v0.4.38 --repo VitalPointAI/near-ai-vscode --pattern '*.vsix' --pattern '*.vsix.sha256' --pattern 'compliance-package-*'
sha256sum --check near-ai-vscode-0.4.38.vsix.sha256
sha256sum --check compliance-package-0.4.38.tar.gz.sha256
unzip -p near-ai-vscode-0.4.38.vsix extension/sbom.cdx.json > extension-sbom.cdx.json
tar -xzf compliance-package-0.4.38.tar.gz
```

To check the SBOM attestation of a rebuilt image, use its digest from the release: `gh attestation verify oci://<image>@<digest> --repo VitalPointAI/near-ai-vscode --predicate-type https://cyclonedx.org/bom`.

The catalogue on this site shows the register as it is on `main`. The register as it was for a given release is in that release's source. Releases made after this catalogue was added also carry it in their assessor package, as `readable/component-inventory.csv` and as inventory items in each system security plan.
